theory.title: When Packets Get Lost
theory.recap: You can route by destination and read firewall rules. This level layers both on top of a new idea: some links silently drop every packet. You'll see all three failure modes at once - a routed path, a firewall-denied path, and a lossy link.
theory.plainObjective: Route to the junction, then identify the path that is both port-allowed and link-stable. Avoid the firewall-denied path and the lossy link.
theory.summary: Network redundancy is why the internet is resilient. Real backbone networks have dozens of alternate paths, and routing protocols automatically reroute traffic around failures - often within seconds.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Networks drop packets
bodyParagraphs.text: IP makes no delivery guarantees. Routers drop packets when links are congested or overloaded. A dropped packet disappears silently - no error, no notification. The sending application must detect the loss and retransmit.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Drop rate
bodyParagraphs.text: Every link has a drop rate - the fraction of packets it silently discards. A 100% drop rate means no packets get through. Unstable links glow red on the canvas. Avoid them.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Three ways to fail
bodyParagraphs.text:
A path can fail three ways:
  • Router refuses to forward (wrong prefix match)
  • Firewall denies your port
  • Link drops the packet silently
All three look like "didn't get through" from outside, but the cause and fix differ.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Redundancy
bodyParagraphs.text: Real networks build multiple paths between the same endpoints. If one link fails, traffic reroutes automatically. Find the stable, allowed path and deliver your packet.

theory.mission:
You carry port 80, destined for 10.0.2.50. R1 routes you to a junction with three exits.

One exit hits a firewall that only allows port 22. Another crosses a link that drops every packet. The third is the stable, allowed path.

termIntroductions.headline: Packet Loss
termIntroductions.body: Networks don't guarantee delivery. Some links are congested, faulty, or overloaded. If a link's drop rate is 100%, every packet crossing it is silently discarded. Look for another path.

termIntroductions.headline: Redundancy
termIntroductions.body: Real networks build multiple paths between endpoints. If one link fails, traffic reroutes automatically. The stable path you just used is why the internet keeps working even when parts of it break.
